nodes.label: grat(1) manual page
nodes.author: phranck
nodes.rationale: The whole manual is rendered by the binary itself (grat manual --markdown), so the documentation always describes the version installed rather than a hand-maintained copy that can drift.

nodes.label: grat.config(7) configuration file
nodes.author: phranck
nodes.rationale: Written as ordinary TOML so it can be read and edited by hand. The file is read as data and only a service's command is ever executed, which keeps a configuration file from being an execution vector beyond the command the author wrote.

nodes.label: grat discover
nodes.rationale: Ports for a batch of marked projects are allocated in a single pass so projects set up together cannot collide with each other or with the existing registry. The searched path is registered as a scan directory in the same step, because a configuration grat cannot find afterwards reserves no port and appears in no status.

nodes.label: grat start
nodes.rationale: A failed start tears down what that command started and removes its state, so a half-started project is never left behind. Ctrl+C takes the same path.

nodes.label: grat stop
nodes.rationale: grat signals only what it can prove is its own, because a process id reused by something else would otherwise be killed. The signal goes to the whole process group, which is what takes descendants such as a Vapor application under swift run with it.

nodes.label: grat recover
nodes.rationale: Adopting managed state written by an older grat lets services from before an upgrade be stopped rather than left running. It never starts anything, and it refuses without a terminal unless --yes is given, because adopting state nobody was shown is a decision nobody made.

nodes.label: grat status
nodes.rationale: Recorded state is validated against the process actually running before anything is reported, so a stale pid file cannot be mistaken for a running service. Exit status 1 on any unhealthy service makes the command usable in a script.

nodes.label: grat ports audit
nodes.rationale: Reports configured collisions and live listeners whilst changing nothing, so the diagnosis is separable from the repair.

nodes.label: grat ports reassign
nodes.rationale: Holds a lock across the scan, the allocation and the writes, so no other grat command can allocate against a registry that is being rewritten. Services are left stopped so their next start picks up the new numbers.

nodes.label: grat update
nodes.rationale: Follows the route that installed the running binary, because replacing a Homebrew-managed file behind Homebrew's back desynchronises the package database. A go install installation is not replaced at all; grat only prints the command.

nodes.label: grat uninstall
nodes.rationale: The .grat directories are grat's own state and go by default, whilst a grat.config is the user's work and survives a reinstall unless removal is asked for.

nodes.label: Background update check
nodes.rationale: The version line comes after the command has done its work so the work never waits on it, the request is capped at two seconds, and every failure is silent because a missing network, a rate limit and an outage all mean the same thing. It asks at most every six hours and GRAT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK turns it off.

nodes.label: Release binary attestation and checksum verification
nodes.rationale: Both the running and the downloaded binary are checked against the published checksums and GitHub's signed attestation before anything is replaced, and the attestation must come from the tagged release workflow on a GitHub-hosted runner. Every address used is restricted to the grat release infrastructure.

nodes.label: How grat decides what a project runs
nodes.rationale: The decisive question is not which framework a project uses but who decides the port, because grat waits for the exact assigned port to be held inside the tree it started. Where the port cannot be established, grat reports the project rather than proposing a command, since a guessed port yields a service that starts, works, and never reports ready, which reads as grat hanging.

nodes.label: Eleventy recognised in order to be refused
nodes.rationale: Its development server binds every interface and its argument parser rejects --host, so nothing keeps the site off the network, and it moves to another port when the assigned one is taken with no equivalent of Vite's --strictPort.

nodes.label: Storybook --exact-port and explicit host
nodes.rationale: Without --exact-port Storybook moves to another port when the assigned one is taken, and the prompt that would ask is suppressed whenever CI is set. The host is stated because Storybook hands its host option straight to listen and never supplies a default.

nodes.label: Spring Boot on Gradle with --no-daemon
nodes.rationale: Gradle runs a build in a long-lived daemon by default, so the application would hang below that daemon rather than below the command grat started; the port is then held outside the tree and readiness never arrives. Spring Boot also reads SERVER_PORT rather than PORT because that is the variable its own binding turns into server.port.

nodes.label: Laravel queue worker detection
nodes.rationale: QUEUE_CONNECTION is read from .env with a fallback to config/queue.php, which is the order Laravel itself resolves it in. The sync connection runs each job in the dispatching process and gets no worker; every other connection gets one, because jobs otherwise wait for a worker that never comes. Nothing else from .env is read and nothing from it reaches a command.

nodes.label: Service roles and their port ranges
nodes.rationale: A service takes its role from its name and the role decides its port range and its readiness rule. Ranges do not overlap so a frontend and a backend of one project never collide, and neither do two projects on one machine. A role names no framework and never changes the configured command.

nodes.label: Port allocation across registered directories
nodes.rationale: Allocation skips every port another configuration reserves and every port a live listener holds, and it covers every project below the registered directories so two projects never receive the same number. The ranges say what grat allocates rather than what a configuration may hold, so an out-of-range port is reported by status without stopping the command.

nodes.label: The environment a command receives
nodes.rationale: A command runs through a non-login /bin/sh that sources no login profile and receives a small non-secret baseline of ten variables, so a service behaves the same however the user's shell is set up. Anything further has to be named in inherit_env and no value is ever stored in grat.config.

nodes.label: BACKEND_URL and backend start ordering
nodes.rationale: Set only where exactly one service carries the backend role, because with none or several the target would be ambiguous. That single backend is started before the services that consume it, and listing the name in inherit_env keeps a value the user set.

nodes.label: PORT owned by grat
nodes.rationale: PORT cannot appear in inherit_env because grat owns it; the assigned number is the one it later waits for.

nodes.label: Readiness contract
nodes.rationale: Three conditions hold at once: the process is alive, the assigned port is held by a process in the tree grat started, and the health path answers in the 200 range. The listener-ownership condition is what stops a service already run by something else from being reported as a success, and it also means a command that hands its work to a background daemon never becomes ready.

nodes.label: Shutdown sequence and process groups
nodes.rationale: Signalling the group rather than the process is what takes descendants with it, such as a Vapor application under swift run, a Vite reload process or a uvicorn reloader. Cancelling during a stop keeps the managed state for a retry and does not escalate from SIGTERM to SIGKILL.

nodes.label: Start identity and managed state
nodes.rationale: grat signals a process only after its live process id, its start identity and its process group all match what was recorded at start, so a process id reused by something else is never signalled. State and logs sit under .grat with restrictive permissions, and a symbolic link in place of the log or either state directory is refused rather than written through, because a repository decides what it brings with it.

nodes.label: Configuration ownership and writability check
nodes.rationale: The upward search for a grat.config stops where a directory belongs to another account, and a file owned by somebody else or writable by its group or everybody is refused by name rather than read. A configuration names commands that run as whoever typed the grat command, so who chose the file is the same question as what it runs.

nodes.label: Sanitisation of names read from project files
nodes.rationale: A name grat reads out of a project's own files, such as an executable target or a directory below cmd, reaches a command only where it is letters, digits, underscore, hyphen or full stop. Anything else is reported with the file and the character rather than written into a command line.

nodes.label: Scan directories
nodes.rationale: A scan looks at most six levels deep because a grat.config sits at a project root, and it never descends into node_modules, vendor, build, dist, target or a framework cache. A registered directory that has been deleted is reported once and skipped rather than refused, because refusing would stop the very command that removes it. Lifecycle commands are unaffected and take the nearest grat.config.

nodes.label: Runtime timing table
nodes.rationale: Every key has a default so the whole table can be left out. Durations are written the way Go writes them, apart from log_tail_lines, which is a count.

nodes.label: The [[services]] table
nodes.rationale: A service is either an HTTP service, which takes a port inside its role's range and answers a health path, or a worker, which has neither and only has to stay alive.

nodes.label: Exit status codes
nodes.rationale: 0 for success, 1 for failure with the reason on standard error, 2 for a wrong command line, and 130 for a cancellation with Ctrl+C.

hyperedges.label: Proving a process is grat's own before signalling it
